headline: Holgate Rip Reshapes on the SW Swell — Fluke Hold the New Drop
subhead: A slow, stubborn south swell rebuilt the bar off the third bowl, and the fluke found the new edge before the rods did.
body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate flat at dead low Tuesday, drone up, coffee going cold in the truck, and the cut that's fed us all summer wasn't sitting where I left it. We've been eating a soft SSW groundswell for close to two weeks now — nothing violent, 2 to 3 feet at six seconds, but steady enough to move sand every single tide cycle. It pushed a new bar up inside the old slough off the third bowl and cut a deeper trough on the ocean side of it than anything we had back in July. That's the kind of quiet reshuffle a lot of guys walk right past. The old spot looks the same from the dune line. It isn't the same underwater, and the fish already know it.

Fluke found that new drop first. I had three keepers and a mess of shorts off the edge of it Wednesday on the last two hours of the outgoing, working a 3/4-oz white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragging it slow off the lip where the trough meets the flat. Water on the ocean side is running warm — the open Atlantic buoy off the coast is reading near 79 degrees — so the fluke are doing exactly what they do this time of year: sitting on the coolest, most current-scrubbed structure they can find instead of baking on the flats. That new Holgate trough qualifies. So does the Little Egg Inlet channel edge on the Holgate side, where the bend narrows the current and doormats have been stacking on the last of the ebb — 5 and 6 pounders coming off there this week on Berkley Gulp in chartreuse, bounced right on bottom in 18 to 22 feet. Graveling Point's channel drop into the Mullica is fishing the same way — cooler, current-swept, holding fish while the surrounding bay flats sit warm and quiet.

Striped bass are a night fishery right now, full stop. Daytime heat has them locked down everywhere except river mouths and hard current seams, and LBI is no exception. The bite window is dawn, dusk, and full dark around bait schools, and Barnegat Light's north jetty has been the most consistent of those windows — bunker spooks and darters worked on the last two hours of the incoming, right where the light current pushes bait against the rocks. Nothing giant, mostly 24 to 30 inches with the occasional overslot mixed in, but it's a real bite if you're willing to fish it at 5 a.m. instead of 5 p.m. Little Egg Inlet mouth has produced the same pattern after dark, plugs worked along the current edge where the inlet dumps into the ocean.

Snapper blues are thick in Great Bay and up into the Mullica creeks, and that's not a surprise — we flagged two weeks back that peanut bunker would push a cocktail blue spike as that bait spread through the back bays, and that's exactly what's happening now. Kids on the docks in Beach Haven and Ship Bottom are having a field day on small Kastmasters and Gotcha plugs, and the adult blues are riding right alongside those bait schools at the inlet mouths — Little Egg and Barnegat Inlet both holding 3 to 5 pound cocktail blues chopping peanut bunker on the surface in the first hour of light. If you see the birds working tight over nervous water at the inlet, that's your invitation. Don't overthink the presentation — a straight metal retrieve through the school is all it takes.

Weakfish are doing the same math. We called this one too — peanut bunker pulling weakfish into the bay system through August — and Graveling Point and the mouth of the Mullica have both given up keeper weakfish this week on bunker chunks and soft plastics fished on the bottom during the last of the outgoing, when the current concentrates that bait against the channel edge. It's not a banner bite, a couple fish an outing if you put the time in, but it's real and it's better than it's been in a couple summers.

Kingfish are scattered through the surf troughs from Ship Bottom down to Holgate, small numbers on bloodworms and Fishbites in the wash, nothing to build a trip around but a nice bonus if you're already out there for fluke or bass. Black drum season on the bay flats has faded — that's a spring pattern and it's closed the book for the year. Tautog stays closed through the summer, as always, so don't waste a drift on the wrecks looking for them.

The moon just came off full, and that extra current strength sharpened the tide-change bites all week — you could feel it pulling harder than normal through the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb. That's going to ease back over the next several days as we move off the full moon, which usually settles the bite windows into a more predictable rhythm rather than the exaggerated push we just had. If I've got one day this week, I'm fishing that new Holgate trough on the outgoing with bucktails, then sliding to Barnegat Light at last light for bass around the bunker. Watch the swell — if it stays in this same soft SSW pattern, expect the sandbars to keep shifting week to week, and the guys who walk the beach and actually look at the cut before they cast are going to keep cashing in on structure nobody else has found yet.
